sections.h2: How does selling a house in Linden, NJ work?
sections.html:
Linden is an industrial and residential city in Union County, roughly 13 miles southwest of Manhattan. Whether an agent lists the house, you handle the sale yourself or a buyer pays cash as-is, the closing ends with a deed filed at the Union County Clerk's office in Elizabeth and the state's transfer fee paid from the seller's side.

Census estimates put Linden at 45,752 residents in mid-2025, which is 4.6% above its April 2020 base. Land area is 10.69 square miles, and another 0.73 square miles is water along the Arthur Kill, the channel that separates the city from Staten Island.

sections.h2: How did Linden develop, and where are its neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Linden was formed as a township on March 4, 1861, from pieces of Elizabeth, Rahway and Union Township. Cranford, Linden Borough and Roselle were later carved out of it. A state act of January 1, 1925 replaced the township and borough with a single city, and linden trees brought from Germany gave it a name.

The population shows how late the growth came: 8,368 people in 1920, 21,206 in 1930, and 39,931 by 1960. Named areas inside the city include Bayway, Grasselli, Tremley, Wheatsheaf, Morses Mill, Vreeland Mills and Warners. The residential section west of St. Georges Avenue is called Sunnyside, named for a former golf club. Linden borders Clark, Cranford, Elizabeth, Rahway, Roselle and Winfield Township in Union County, plus Carteret and Woodbridge across the county line.

Linden is also a regional center of Polish settlement. About 13.1% of residents report Polish origin, and the city holds an annual Polish Heritage Day Festival.

sections.h2: What does the Census show for Linden's homes and households?
sections.html:
Owners occupy 59.5% of Linden homes, and 36.1% of residents were born outside the country. The middle owner-occupied home is valued at $419,700.

sections.h2: What industry and employers shape Linden's housing market?
sections.html:
Linden's eastern edge runs along the Arthur Kill, a waterway used for bulk cargo shipping. The Bayway Refinery, a Phillips 66 facility, turns out about 230,000 barrels of petroleum products a day. For 2022 the Census lists about $517 million of transportation and warehousing revenue and $1.53 billion in retail sales.

General Motors ran Linden Assembly from 1937 to 2005, and most of the plant was later torn down for a redevelopment on a 100-acre site. Merck, one of the larger pharmaceutical companies in the country, is based across Linden and Rahway.

Transit shapes how buyers look at Linden houses. The Census puts the average commute at 31.5 minutes. Main options:

  • Rail: Linden station offers a one-seat ride to Manhattan in 39 minutes on the North Jersey Coast Line and Northeast Corridor Line.
  • Highways: the New Jersey Turnpike runs through the east side, Interstate 278 ends in Linden, and U.S. 1/9 and Route 27 cross the city. The Garden State Parkway runs about 500 feet beyond the western city line.
  • Bus: NJ Transit routes 112 and 115 run to Manhattan's Port Authority, and routes 48 and 94 serve Elizabeth and Newark.
  • Air: Newark Liberty is roughly a 15-minute drive, and Linden Airport takes small general aviation flights.

A house near the station should say so up front in any listing or offer request.

sections.h2: Which Linden neighborhoods and amenities come up with buyers?
sections.html:
Sunnyside is the residential area west of St. Georges Avenue, named for a former golf club, and it borders Clark, Cranford and Winfield on the west and Roselle on the east. Bayway, Tremley, Wheatsheaf and Grasselli are other named areas inside the city. The Raymond Wood Bauer Promenade hosts outdoor concerts in warm weather.

  • 85.7% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so many neighbors are long-term owners and renters.
  • 15.0% of residents are 65 or older and 20.4% are under 18, a mix that spans retirees and school-age families.
  • 23.3% of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher, and 70.8% of people 16 and over are in the labor force.
  • Retail sales for 2022 work out to $35,380 per resident.

Those Census figures describe who lives in Linden today: long-tenured households with rail and bus links to Newark, Elizabeth and Manhattan.

sections.h2: What are the public schools in Linden?
sections.html: Linden Public Schools serve prekindergarten through grade 12 with 11 schools and 6,125 students in 2022-23. Eight elementary schools (Schools 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10) cover PreK to grade 5, McManus Middle School and Soehl Middle School cover grades 6 to 8, and Linden High School had 1,801 students. School No. 5 was named a National Blue Ribbon School in 2020. Families will ask which numbered school covers your block, so find out before you list.

sections.h2: What local steps does a Linden seller handle before closing?
sections.html:
Call the City of Linden's construction and code office and ask which paperwork is due before closing: a continued certificate of occupancy, a fire inspection or a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. Ask about open permits on the property too, and request the answers in writing for the buyer's attorney.

Recordings for Linden go to the Union County Clerk at 2 Broad Street, Elizabeth (908-527-4787). The recording office keeps weekday hours of 8:30 to 4:30, takes over-the-counter filings until 3:30, and needs no appointment. Online land records cover June 1, 1977 onward, and a free property fraud alert program emails or calls subscribers when their name shows up on a recorded document.

At a median value of $419,700, a typical Linden sale falls in the state's schedule for prices above $350,000, where the rate rises in steps with the price. Residential deeds above $1 million also carry a percentage fee. The seller bears both charges.

sections.h2: When does a cash purchase suit a Linden house?
sections.html:
When the house needs work, has tenants, or must close by a fixed date. Paying cash as-is takes repair requests and mortgage approval out of the schedule. A listing can still bring a higher price for a house in good condition, since it reaches owner-occupants and investors.

Get written terms from every buyer and compare line by line: price, closing date, who pays the transfer fee and who handles any city inspection. Two offers with the same headline number can leave you with different amounts at the table. Keep the survey, tax bills and any permit paperwork in one folder, and ask your title company for a copy of your recorded deed.

faqs.q: Will Linden's city office inspect my house before I sell?
faqs.a: Ask the City of Linden's construction and code office. Resale rules vary by town in New Jersey, so get written confirmation of any certificate your address needs and how long scheduling takes.

faqs.q: Who bears the transfer fee in a Linden sale?
faqs.a: The seller. It is calculated on the deed price and paid when the Union County Clerk records the deed. Sales over $1 million add a graduated percent fee, also on the seller.

faqs.q: Which office handles recording for Linden deeds?
faqs.a: The Union County Clerk's recording office, 2 Broad Street, Elizabeth. Recording takes no appointment.

faqs.q: Can a Linden rental or two-family house sell with tenants in it?
faqs.a: Yes. Give the buyer the leases and rent roll, and ask the city whether a rental registration or inspection is tied to the property. Confirm in writing whether each buyer will take the house with tenants in place.

faqs.q: How fast can a Linden house sale close?
faqs.a: Speed depends on who buys and on city paperwork. Without mortgage underwriting a cash deal can move sooner, but deed recording and any required city certificate still take their own time.
